title: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead
hook: the shortest gospel, the mountain ahead; "the beginning of the good news"

segments.voice: Yesterday: the church, the people, not the building. Now the whole camp, quickly: communion, the Trinity, born again, baptism, testimony, the Holy Spirit, the Bible, amen, grace, Jesus, the Lord's Prayer, the Good Samaritan, the Prodigal Son, the Beatitudes, love, faith, the Psalms, the cross, Easter, the church. Twenty words. Today makes twenty-one.
screen: `FIND TWO OR THREE.` → the strand, twenty words lit.

segments.voice: So many of those words lead back to four short books: the Gospels. Matthew, Mark, Luke and John. On day seven you heard that a lot of people start reading the Bible with a Gospel. The shortest of the four is Mark. Sixteen chapters. You could read the whole thing aloud in one sitting, in somebody's living room. It's fast. It's blunt. It skips the parts you'd expect. There's no Christmas in it, no shepherds, no star. It starts with a man shouting in the desert. And its very first line is today's word.
screen: `FOUR SHORT BOOKS.` → `MARK: THE SHORTEST.` → `NO CHRISTMAS. A DESERT.` → `THE FIRST LINE.`

segments.voice: Mark, chapter one, verse one. In the old English: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole verse. It's a title, and a door. Start with gospel: good news. Mark's Greek word is euangelion, and it wasn't a church word yet. Historians point to Roman-era inscriptions that use it for public announcements: a victory won, news about an emperor, news that changes the day for everyone who hears it. Mark takes that word and puts it on a builder from Galilee. Now the shape, so you know the mountain ahead. First, Galilee: a man baptized in a river, fishermen dropping their nets, healings, arguments, and the stories he told. A word Mark uses again and again here is straightway. Immediately. Everything happens fast. Then, right in the middle, the turning point. Jesus asks his friends: who do you say that I am? And from there the road turns toward Jerusalem. The last third of the book is one week: the entry into the city, the table and the bread, the cross, and the empty tomb, where the women run away, afraid. Which brings us back to the book's first word. Beginning. Some readers notice that Mark calls all of it, the whole book, just the beginning. As if the good news isn't finished when the book ends. As if the reader is supposed to pick it up from there.
screen: `EUANGELION — GOOD NEWS.` · `GALILEE: STRAIGHTWAY.` · `THE TURN: WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?` · `ONE LAST WEEK.` · then, large: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOOD NEWS.`

segments.voice: Last sit of the camp. Sit, and breathe, the way you did on day one, when the first word was communion, a meal that remembers. Now let one word from these three weeks come back to you on its own. Don't pick it. Let it arrive. Grace, maybe. Or the stone already moved. Or small is enough. Hold it for a few breaths. Then ask, gently: where does this start for me? If you pray, you can offer that word back as your prayer, with an amen. If you don't, just hold it, and let it be a beginning.
Mark 1:1. The beginning of the gospel: good news, and only the beginning of it. Twenty-first word, and the strand is complete.
screen: `MARK 1:1 — your 21st word` → the strand complete → `CAMP 1. FIRST WORDS. DONE.`

segments.voice: Your line: start here. Tomorrow, Camp 2 begins with the stories, and why he told them at all. Three weeks, done.

howItsDone: Christians hear the Gospels read aloud in church, and some churches follow a cycle of readings in which one year draws largely on Mark. Some groups read the whole of Mark aloud in one sitting.

fork.setup: you're writing a Gospel. everyone wants to know about this man. where do you begin?
options: with his birth in Bethlehem and a star.
with the beginning of the world.
with a man shouting in the desert, and a title: the beginning of the gospel.
fork.reveal: Mark skips the birth entirely. "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ" — and then straight into the desert. fast, blunt, no Christmas.

original.note: Greek, Mark 1:1: the beginning of the good news. the first words of the shortest Gospel.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chapter-and-verse number.
what it means: the first line of the shortest Gospel — a title that calls the whole book only the beginning of the good news.
what a scholar hears: archē, beginning, is the book's first word. and euangelion, before it was a church word, could announce public good news, like a victory.

sources.quoted: The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God

notes: Review 2026-10-01: cut 'most scholars think' (now 'some scholars'), 'about forty years', 'about two hours' and 'the way the first Christians probably heard it'; 'every word you just said comes from the Gospels' corrected; Old English godspel aside and its match pair removed; 'favorite word' softened to a word Mark uses again and again; 'the oldest copies end' (manuscript claim) replaced by what 16:8 says; trapdoor's Mark 1:1 manuscript note replaced; fork no longer assumes Mark was written first.
'The Son of God' in Mark 1:1 is missing from some early manuscripts (e.g. the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus); not mentioned in the spoken lines.
KJV Mark 1:1 ends with a semicolon ('the Son of God;'); quoted without it.
Euangelion in imperial use (e.g. the Priene calendar inscription for Augustus's birthday) summarized without quotation.
Mark's frequent 'straightway / immediately' (Greek euthys, some forty times); the KJV renders it variously (straightway, immediately, forthwith).
Greek in 'original' is the opening phrase ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου; pronunciation given in an Erasmian-leaning style — please check. Could instead be the single word εὐαγγέλιον.
